title: Supreme Court Cancels Probation for Convicts in Brutal 2003 Bahraich Attack
excerpt: Justices Pardiwala and Chandran held that the High Court granted probation under the Probation of Offenders Act despite an adverse probation report and without weighing the nature of the offence, and ordered both men to surrender within two weeks.
body:
• The Supreme Court set aside the Allahabad High Court's probation order for two men convicted in a 2003 knife and gun attack in Bahraich and directed them to surrender within two weeks.
  • Justices J.B. Pardiwala and K. Vinod Chandran faulted the High Court for granting Section 4 probation despite an adverse probation officer's report and the brutality of the offence.
  • The trial court had convicted both men under Section 308 IPC and sentenced each to five years' rigorous imprisonment and a Rs 20,000 fine.
  • Their criminal appeals return to the High Court at Lucknow, to be heard only after the convicts are in custody.

The Supreme Court has set aside an Allahabad High Court order that released on probation two men convicted in a 2003 knife and gun attack in Uttar Pradesh's Bahraich district, criticising the High Court for extending the benefit out of "misplaced sympathy" despite the brutality of the crime, Press Trust of India reported via News89. The Court directed the convicts to surrender within two weeks, failing which the Additional Sessions Court in Bahraich must immediately begin proceedings to apprehend them.

A bench of Justices J.B. Pardiwala and K. Vinod Chandran faulted the High Court for applying Section 4 of the Probation of Offenders Act, 1958 on the ground that the accused were first-time offenders, without considering the brutality of the crime and the serious injuries suffered by the victim.

"The accused have gone scot-free without suffering a single day of imprisonment, especially by reason of the misplaced sympathy based on grandiose expositions of law, totally inapplicable to the facts of the case."

Context & Background

The case arose from a business rivalry after the complainant opened a shop near that of the accused in Bahraich. On the day of the incident, one accused was armed with a cutting weapon and the other with a gun. They attacked the victim, caused severe injuries and left him unconscious before he was taken to Bahraich Hospital. The trial court convicted the two men under Section 308 of the Indian Penal Code, for attempt to commit culpable homicide not amounting to murder, and sentenced each to five years' rigorous imprisonment and a fine of Rs 20,000, according to LawChakra's account of the judgment in Umesh Chand v. State of U.P. and Others, dated October 7, 2026.

The High Court upheld the conviction but granted Section 4 probation, directing each man to execute a personal bond of Rs 20,000 and keep the peace and be of good behaviour for one year, relying on the roughly 22 years since the incident and the absence of earlier convictions. The informant, the brother of the injured man, then moved the Supreme Court. Before the Supreme Court, the State disclosed the accused's criminal antecedents and a proposal for preventive action under the U.P. Control of Goondas Act, 1970. The Probation Officer's report listed several cases against both men, including matters still pending trial, and recorded the victim's lasting injuries, among them a nearly severed right thumb, scarring, chronic pain and continuing treatment in Lucknow. Those pending cases are allegations that remain untested.

Impact/Analysis

The bench held that the circumstances of the case, including the nature of the offence and the character of the offender, must be the reigning factor in deciding whether release on good conduct is expedient, and that this was lacking here. It said it could not understand why the High Court observed the accused had been suffering for 22 years when they had remained on bail and were "merrily indulging in criminal activities", and it criticised the casual manner in which both the trial court and the High Court handled the case. The Court also criticised the trial court for framing a charge under Section 308 instead of Section 307, which deals with attempt to murder, observing that the victim's injuries appeared to amount to grievous hurt, while noting that little could be done on the charge at this stage.

Section 4 lets a court release a convict on probation of good conduct instead of sentencing, but requires the court to weigh the nature of the offence and the character of the offender, and to consider the Probation Officer's report where one is available. The ruling reiterates that the lapse of time or a clean conviction record is not enough on its own when that report points the other way.

What's Next

The two convicts must surrender within two weeks. If they do not, the Additional Sessions Court at Bahraich, which conducted the trial, is to take immediate steps to apprehend them. Their criminal appeals stand restored before the Allahabad High Court at Lucknow, which the Supreme Court requested to take up the appeals only after ensuring the accused are taken into custody. Pending applications stand rejected.
